To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dynein uses a novel powerstroke mechanism that involves a large domain at its base, the linker, that moves in a complex way to generate force.
dynein moves along microtubule tracks in a unique way, which is different from kinesin and myosin, and that the dynein stalk acts like a flexible lever to amplify the force generated at its base.

(1) the dynein powerstroke is produced through ATP-induced remodellings of the linker domain; (2) the microtubules are bound through a small domain located at the tip of the stalk; (3) the dyneins move in an unusual sliding mode; and (4) the dyneinin dimer walks processively by an unusual sliding mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how dynein moves along microtubule tracks to perform its diverse cellular roles.
the mechanism of movement of molecular machines, in particular the dynein microtubule motor.
the structure, function, and regulation of molecular motors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dynein molecular motor has a unique structure and mechanism of operation.
the structure and mechanism of the dynein motors is not well understood.
dyneins move in a manner that has never been observed before.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have solved the crystal structure of the dynein stalk and motor domains and have determined how they interact with each other and with the microturbule.
the crystallographic studies have provided the most detailed insights into the structure and function of the dynein microtubule motor to date.
dynein has evolved an ingenious mechanism that allows it to power its movement by a small domain that can be readily regulated by other parts of the protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dynein linker is the key component that drives the power stroke.
dynein is a remarkably sophisticated motor protein.
dynein has a unique and complex way to move.
